newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND-1996 a hard year to follow for Eurobourses.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-1996 a hard year to follow for Eurobourses.

text.p: After an exhilarating 1996, most European bourses will find next year's performance a more sober affair as economies begin to stray from the golden path of low growth, inflation and interest rates, strategists say.
An unholy scenario of a pick-up in the economic cycle coupled with the increasing risk of fall-out from a U.S. stock market correction will pose a threat to European markets.
With the added pressure on governments to meet Maastricht targets in the run-up to the first wave of monetary union, Europe may soon begin to feel the strain, strategists warn.
"The returns don't look so great for next year," said Jerry Evans, European strategist at Swedish brokerage Enskilda. "After a phenomenal year the outlook is generally more cautious."

Taken from current index levels and average forecasts from a Reuters poll of global stock market expectations, analysts expect the biggest percentage gains to be seen on Milan's BCI general index and Madrid's Ibex-35, with gains seen of up to 16 percent.
But Europe's most active stock market is expected to be a laggard. The UK's FT-SE 100 is seen rising around 5 percent, far below the nine percent seen so far in 1996.
The main risk to equity markets over the coming year will be from a general pick-up in growth, putting upward pressure on inflation and interest rates.

But strategists also warn of possible fall-out from a major U.S. correction which some have been expecting for some time. The Dow has left its European counterparts behind to race over 28 percent ahead this year.
"We have no doubt that in the event of a significant correction in the U.S. European markets would suffer as well," said David Aserkoff, strategist at CS First Boston.
Richard Davidson at Morgan Stanley has one of the most pessimistic outlooks for European equities in 1997. He advises investors to protect against risks of a major setback.

"Markets are displaying all the classical signs of a peak in the bull market...We believe European equity markets will correct from their peaks and finish 1997 up to 10 percent lower than today," he said in a recent research note.
Davidson predicts that the UK's FTSE 100 and Italy's BCI index will be the only ones to show percentage gains next year from his expected 1996 year-end levels.
He expects Milan's index to nudge just 1.9 percent higher in 1997 and the UK's FTSE to show a mere one percent rise.

A central theme running through all of Europe's markets will be convergence to Maastricht targets and the make-up of the first wave of participants in EMU. It is likely to be the priority for countries such as Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands, says Enskilda's Evans.

"In light of the tight fiscal policy environment, growth is likely to be modest and interest rates will stay lower for longer." said Evans. "Softening currencies will mean industrial recovery which will be export driven, but this growth should not be enough to stir inflation."
Evans targets Germany's DAX index as a likely outperformer. Average forecasts point to the DAX rising 6 percent in 1997.

France, troubled by the impact of social unrest resulting from the government's Maastricht-led austerity measures, is unlikely to be among the star performers. The CAC index has still not breached its 1994 peak.

The stimulus for London's FTSE is seen coming from growth and profits, but strategists warn that the full impact of a stronger currency has not yet been seen. Sterling has risen to four-year highs against the mark and the dollar this year.

Most strategists are also unwilling to take a bullish stance on the UK bourse ahead of a general election in the UK. The ruling Conservative government was trailing the opposition Labour Party by 22 points in the latest MORI opinion poll.
As with the UK, Sweden and Denmark look increasingly unlikely to join the first wave of EMU and a risk premium is already being factored into these markets.

"The risk premium explains why the Italian lira bond is valued more highly than a sterling bond for the first time in 30 years, why sterling is becoming a one-way bet and why UK interest rates are double those in Germany." Evans said.

European Monetary Union also explains why Italy and Spain represent risky bets for investors. The forecasts of 15 percent gains assume both countries will enter the first wave of EMU which led one strategist to describe these bourses as "either the biggest gainers or the biggest losers."

Most strategists assume that Spain will put in a good performance as its interest rate-sensitive market is continued to be pushed by interest rate positive sentiment. The general index is expected to add 16 percent from today's levels.

Yet if Davidson's pessimistic scenario for Eurobourses transpires then he points out that Italy is historically one of the best performing markets during European corrections although it remains one of the most volatile.

Davidson suggests "picking the low-volatility markets, the markets that have outperformed in previous corrections and the markets with a stronger fundamental case," to cover risks. On a fundamental basis the strategist prefers UK and Germany.
